title: The Traction Circle: Turning, Speeding Up and Braking Share One Budget of Grip, and a Vehicle That Spends It All on One Has Nothing Left for the Others

questions.question: What does the friction circle say?
options: Turning, speeding up and braking share one budget of grip
Each tyre has its own limit, used separately
Braking is limited by the brakes, turning by the steering
questions.explanation: The tyres give one total, the friction times g. The sideways and the fore and aft accelerations have to fit inside it together, as the two sides of a right triangle.

questions.question: At 1.5 m/s round the smallest circle on gravel, the turn took what share of the grip?
questions.explanation: The sideways acceleration is the speed squared over the radius, 3.03 m/s2, against a grip of 4.41 m/s2 on gravel.

questions.question: The most the vehicle could brake fell from 4.81 m/s2 to:
questions.explanation: With 69 percent of the grip in the turn, the root of what remains is left for braking. Speeding up fell from 4.02 to 2.82 m/s2.

questions.question: At which speed did the turn alone use all the grip?
questions.explanation: Where the turn's acceleration equals the grip: the root of friction times g times the radius. Above it the vehicle cannot even hold its speed.

questions.question: At 99 percent of the sliding speed, how much of the straight line braking was left?
questions.explanation: The turn takes 0.99 squared, 98 percent, of the grip. The root of one less 0.98 squared is 0.20.

questions.question: What should a planner do about a bend it will meet at speed?
options: Brake hardest at the tightest point
Hold its speed and steer more
Speed up to shorten the time in the bend
Slow before it, because the bend leaves little to brake with
questions.explanation: In the bend most of the grip is spent on turning. Braking there adds to a budget already used, and the vehicle slides.
